newsitem.title: CANADA: Last of GM's 26,000 Canadian workers set to walk out.
newsitem.headline: Last of GM's 26,000 Canadian workers set to walk out.

text.p: The last of 26,000 General Motors Corp. unionized workers are set to walk out at midnight on Wednesday, bringing all of the carmaker's plants in Canada to a standstill.

Canadian Auto Workers (CAW) union President Buzz Hargrove said workers at GM's Woodstock, Ontario, parts distribution plant, about 60 miles (150 km) southwest of Toronto, had already walked off the job ahead of the 11:59 p.m. EDT (3:59 a.m. GMT) strike deadline.
He said workers began striking after GM asked them to load extra train boxcars with auto parts ahead of tonight's strike.

"I understand the Woodstock parts people walked off the job because the company was trying to move out a number of train carloads of parts in preparation for a long strike," Hargrove said. "The word out of Windsor it is going to be difficult to keep people on the (production) lines."

GM Canada spokesman Stew Low acknowleged the company had accepted that by midnight on Wednesday all of the remaining 6,350 unionized workers at GM plants in London, Woodstock and Windsor, Ontario, will walk off the job.

Neither side has shown any sign of budging in the stand-off that started on Oct. 3 when the CAW began a series of escalating strikes with a walkout at GM plants in Oshawa, Ontario, and Ste. Therese, Quebec, and continued a walkout at the carmaker's St. Catharines, Ontario, plant on Sunday.

The dispute has centred on GM's ability to shift work to outside, usually non-unionized companies -- a practice known as outsourcing -- that would cut 5,500 union jobs at GM's Canadian operations. Wages and work rules have also been at issue.

Hargrove said negotiations had been hijacked by GM's top executives in the United States, adding that he believes GM's chief executive officer, Jack Smith, wants to test the resolve of the CAW ahead of any possible settlement with the United Autoworkers Union in America.
"I am resigned to the fact that this thing is going to sit for a few days," Hargrove said.

In Detroit, Smith told reporters on Wednesday that the Canadian labour pact must allow the carmaker to become competitive. "We've got certain things that will cripple the company if we don't get (it) fixed right," Smith said.
"We are focused on getting a settlement," GM Canada's Low added, noting that a full strike increases pressure on both parties to get a deal.
"It puts more pressure on because you have 26,000 people out of work," he said.
Hargrove has said he and GM Canada lead negotiator Dean Munger have continued to meet daily, but the meetings usually degenerate into shouting matches.

With the strike going into its eigth day on Thursday, some GM plants in the United States have already been idled and workers were told to stay home for the third straight day. GM is expected to halt production at more plants this week as they fall short of components made in Canada.
Some analysts said the world's largest automaker will try to wait out the strike, hoping to deplete the union's $37 million strike fund.
"They will go as long as it takes," one analyst said in Toronto.

But Hargrove has said the union's strike fund could last at least 12 weeks and stretch to 16 weeks if new credit is arranged. The CAW also has set a special meeting for Oct. 18 to raise funds from all its 210,000 members across Canada.
"GM can't out wait us," Hargrove said Tuesday. "We're not going anywhere."
Analysts said GM did not want to give in to the CAW while negotiations continued with the United Auto Workers (UAW) union in the United States.
"They (GM) are not about to give Canada (workers) a relatively generous deal while they are negotiating in the U.S.," said Denis Desrosier, president of Desrosier Automotive Consultants Inc.
